## How far does a random walker get? {#title .title-card}

::: {.subtitle}
The mean squared displacement, defined and measured on simulated walkers
:::

::: {.byline}
A. Author · An Institute
:::

::: {.art}
{{< include build/fig/walkers.html >}}
:::

::: say
Release a crowd of walkers from one point, and let each take random steps.
:::

::: say
How far do they get? This short talk defines the quantity that answers that, and then measures it.
:::

## The mean squared displacement {#define sec="The quantity"}

<!-- A slide laid out by hand, as a custom scene of the video is: each block is pinned at the engine's x and 1 - y
     (per cent of the frame) and sized in its points (.s22 = 22 points). -->

::: {.absolute .fig left="5%" top="18%" width="42%" height="66%"}
{{< include build/fig/walker.html >}}
:::

::: {.say grow="#walker-path"}
Follow a single walker. Its path is erratic, and it returns again and again.
:::

::: {.absolute .s22 .muted left="5.5%" top="16.6%"}
one walker, {{< meta v.shown >}} steps
:::

::: {.say point="#walker-dr"}
After a time t it has moved by a displacement, the arrow.
:::

::: {.say point="#msd-def"}
We square the length of that arrow, and average it over all walkers. That is the mean squared displacement.
:::

::: {#msd-def .absolute .s34 left="56%" top="28.4%"}
$\langle\Delta r^2\rangle(t)=\dfrac{1}{N}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}\left|\Delta\mathbf{r}_i(t)\right|^2$
:::

::: {.absolute .s24 .muted left="56%" top="43.7%"}
the squared displacement after a time t,\
averaged over all N walkers
:::

::: say
For diffusion it grows in proportion to time, with a slope of four times the diffusion constant.
:::

::: {.absolute .takeaway left="55.7%" top="57.7%"}
Diffusion: ⟨Δr²⟩ = 4 D t in two dimensions
:::

::: {.note}
Simulated walkers: independent Gaussian steps, D = {{< meta v.D0 >}} in units of step length squared per step.
:::

::: say
Here is the mean squared displacement of our {{< meta v.walkers >}} walkers, against time.
:::

- Points: the average over {{< meta v.walkers >}} walkers

::: {.say point="#msd-fit"}
A straight line fits it. Its slope gives a diffusion constant of {{< meta v.D >}}.
:::

- Line: a least-squares fit through the origin

::: say
So in twice the time the crowd covers twice the area, and the measurement returns the constant we put in.
:::

- Twice the time, twice the area covered

::: {.takeaway}
The slope returns the D we put in
:::
:::::
::::

::: {.note}
{{< meta v.walkers >}} simulated walkers, {{< meta v.steps >}} steps, one seed; the line is a least-squares fit.
:::

## A random walker's reach grows as the square root of time {#summary sec="Summary"}

<!-- The video's bullet_scene(): staged bullets only. -->

::: say
To summarise. The mean squared displacement measures how far a crowd of walkers gets.
:::

- The mean squared displacement measures how far a crowd of walkers gets

::: say
For diffusion it is a straight line in time, and its slope is four times the diffusion constant.
:::

- For diffusion it is a straight line in time, with slope 4D

::: say
The typical distance is its square root. A random walker's reach therefore grows only as the square root of time. Thank you for your attention.
:::

- Its square root, the typical distance, grows only as the square root of time
